description: Probes protected by .NET Reactor 7.5.0.0, built by corpus/probes/build.sh rather than collected, so each protected entry has its unprotected self beside it as an oracle -- the ground truth the malware profiles cannot have. Detection now reports the version-honest token 'reactor' rather than 'reactor6': the tool identifies the .NET Reactor family and its generation (jit-hook or delegate-runtime) from structure, but no structural signal separates Reactor 6 from 7.5 -- these probes carry the same clrjit/m_pData/RuntimeModule strings the Reactor 6 corpus does, getJit never appears in plaintext in either, and the only thing unique to these files is the Eziriz unregistered-trial watermark, a licence artifact absent from registered builds. So a 'reactor' verdict here is correct, not a mislabel; it simply does not claim a version the tool cannot prove. The strings-only configuration is now recognised too (reactor at 60%, on the strength of its protected-string resolver plus dispatcher and dead-call junk) where it was previously discarded as 'none' at 40% against the 0.55 gate, and it now recovers in full on all three target frameworks: every protected-string call site is replaced with its plaintext and the recovered strings match the oracle byte for byte. The .NET Framework build was already recovered by the resolver shape shared with Reactor 6; the CoreCLR builds inline the table-framing loop into the resolver and load the decrypted resource out of line through a one-argument (object stream) loader rather than the two-argument (stream, offset) initializer the Framework build uses, so the capture now also recognises that loader by shape and runs it on the resource stream to fill the same blob field the framing reads. probe-*-strings pin that recovery (full string-site coverage plus the one constant decoder site); the encrypted-resource bundle those builds also carry is a separate feature that stays unrecovered, which is why one pass reports unsupported without failing the run. The .NET Framework full configuration now recovers in full as well (see probe-net48-full below); the CoreCLR necrobit builds still recover nothing and remain exploratory, but the .NET Framework necrobit build now recovers in full. On .NET Framework, method-body recovery installs Reactor 7's getJit-based JIT hook -- the getJit native delegate returns a modelled vtable-backed ICorJitCompiler, so the loader gets past acquiring the JIT -- and the earlier belief that it then decrypts inside the JIT callback from live memory was wrong: NecroBit decrypts every protected body up front during module initialisation into a managed Hashtable keyed by each method's IL address, and its compileMethod hook only copies the already-decrypted bytes out. The loader interpretation stops where it turns to installing the native hook (a Marshal.ReadInt32 of a live-JIT address that lies in no modelled region), but by then the table is full, so probe-net48-necrobit is recovered by reading that table out of the interpreter heap, mapping each entry back to its method by the single module base that lines every key up with a protected stub's IL RVA, and grafting the plaintext. The locals-signature token and, for the one body that had them, the exception clauses are not in the table: NecroBit zeroes each protected method's LocalVarSigTok and stubs its header, then restores them at load time with the same deterministic mapped-image writes the Reactor 6 path already replays -- a four-byte write of the real StandAloneSig token into each fat header and a flags write that re-sets the more-sections bit -- and the exception section itself is left in the image at the offset the JIT computes from the stub's own code size. So recovery replays those header writes to recover the frame and reads the section back to reattach the handlers, and probe-net48-necrobit pins all thirteen bodies coming back with zero stubs remaining, its ComputeChecksum carrying its four locals and its ReadEmbeddedSecret its two finally clauses. probe-net48-full now recovers in full: it recovers all 680 of its bodies the same way the necrobit build does, resolves the delegate-proxy map by running the Reactor 7 resolver itself and seeding the 142 decoded bindings so the proxy call sites become direct calls, and then reads its extra virtualization layer end to end. Naming the two operations the loader initializer leaves unread (an int32->Byte[] table load and a forced net -1) lets the engine's own numbering be learned, and the operations the string table's second serialized program uses but the initializer never does -- a unary integer operator and an instance-field store -- are named from that program's own census before the reading, so the serialized evaluator performs every operation and captures the table under this build's numbering. The date-based trial guard the loader injects, which reads the wall clock through a proxy and throws when the arbitrary instant the interpreter injects falls outside its window, is recognised by shape and neutralised during interpretation so it no longer ends the run. All 20 protected-string call sites are then restored and the recovered strings match the oracle. It pins those 680 bodies coming back with no stubs left, full string-site coverage, every virtual operation read as IL with a stack walk that agrees with itself, and the virtualized method built back into the cleaned copy. Neutralising the guard also lets the module's own bundle reader run to the end, so the encrypted managed-resource bundle is decrypted statically and pinned by the SHA-256 of its 2048-byte plaintext (the same Probe.Secret.txt and Probe.g.resources streams the necrobit oracle carries); before the guard was handled the reader stopped in the module initializer and produced only partial buffers that parsed as nothing. The one pass that still reports unsupported without failing the run is payload-extraction, because this probe packs no from-memory assembly for it to recover. On CoreCLR the necrobit builds recover nothing and stay exploratory: there the loader does not fill a managed table but patches JITted native code directly through process memory (on Linux, /proc/self/mem), a mechanism this static reading does not model; probe-net80-necrobit and probe-net100-necrobit pin that they are still detected as reactor without their bodies coming back. The CoreCLR full builds answer RuntimeInformation.IsOSPlatform from the profile (Windows), read their own AssemblyName.Version and manifest module, and run on to roughly 18 million steps before stopping on FieldInfo.GetValue over a runtime-internal field, where the loader is reflecting an IntPtr[] of method-table pointers out of live runtime state; probe-net80-full and probe-net100-full pin the FieldInfo.GetValue stop, so a regression that reintroduced the get_Version or get_ManifestModule gaps fails here. Three target frameworks from one source separate those causes. Caveat on scale: the probe has few methods, so the detector's ten-stub and ten-proxy thresholds sit near the edge in the necrobit-only configuration and its confidence there says as much about probe size as about Reactor 7.
